edges.description: The variant protein is either not made, not secreted, or secreted in a form that cannot act as a prothrombinase cofactor.
Less circulating functional factor V means less factor Va available to serve as the prothrombinase cofactor.
Less functional prothrombinase converts less prothrombin to thrombin.
Insufficient thrombin to convert fibrinogen to fibrin at the rate a haemostatic plug requires.
A slowly formed or unstable clot fails to secure haemostasis, producing spontaneous and provoked bleeding.
The most feared complication, concentrated in neonates and infants with the lowest factor V levels.
Locally released platelet factor V/Va supports thrombin generation at the platelet surface despite absent plasma factor V.
Lower TFPI lifts the inhibitory brake on the initiating tissue-factor complex, reducing the factor V requirement for thrombin generation.
edges.source: Low Plasma Tissue Factor Pathway Inhibitor

edges.description: Complete absence of factor V produces fatal spontaneous bleeding, reproducing the organism-level bleeding tendency.
edges.limitations: Total factor V deficiency is embryonic or perinatally lethal in the mouse, whereas human disease is a survivable chronic diathesis in which some residual factor V (plasma or platelet) is essentially always present. The model cannot report the human natural history, genotype-phenotype relation, or long-term treatment, and its lethality is why human complete deficiency is so rare.

edges.description: Minimal liver-directed factor V expression rescues the otherwise fatal bleeding of the null mouse, modelling the viability threshold rather than the symptomatic human phenotype.
edges.limitations: The transgene is expressed from a heterologous promoter at a fixed low level, not from the native locus, so it tests a viability threshold rather than reproducing any particular human genotype or its bleeding pattern.

edges.description: A missense knock-in reproduces the reduced circulating factor V activity and the prolonged clotting times of mild human disease in a viable animal.
edges.limitations: The model carries one engineered missense allele chosen for mildness, so it represents the mild end of the spectrum and does not reproduce severe or null-allele disease or its intracranial-haemorrhage risk.

edges.description: Loss of fv delays clot occlusion after vascular injury, reproducing the impaired clot formation of the human disease in a screenable vertebrate.
edges.limitations: Zebrafish tolerate factor V loss longer than mammals, and the paper reports an apparently dominant pattern in the fish, so the inheritance and timing do not transfer to the human disease; the model is best read as a variant/drug-screening tool rather than a faithful clinical model.

edges.description: FV:C measures the functional consequence of the genetic lesion at the level of circulating protein activity, and defines the conventional severity strata.

nodes.description: Umbilical cord bleeding, a neonatal presenting sign of severe deficiency.

evidence.reference_title: Congenital coagulation factor V deficiency with intracranial hemorrhage.
evidence.snippet: Umbilical bleeding, anterior fontanelle tensed

nodes.description: Tranexamic acid, used for mucosal and minor bleeding and as cover for minor procedures. It does not correct the coagulation defect; it protects the clot that does form from premature lysis, so it is adjunctive.

evidence.reference_title: Factor V deficiency: a concise review.
evidence.snippet: Antifibrinolytics can also provide benefit, especially for mucosal bleeding.

nodes.description: Homozygous or compound heterozygous variants in F5 on chromosome 1q24. Missense substitutions predominate; the reported spectrum also includes nonsense, frameshift, splice-site and large-deletion alleles, with more than two thirds of the published severe-deficiency alleles being null mutations that reduce factor V expression.

cell_types: hepatocyte, the principal site of factor V synthesis

evidence.reference_title: Factor V deficiency.
evidence.snippet: A total of 56 mutations have been published to date as being responsible for severe or moderately severe FV deficiency; more than two thirds of these are null mutations (mainly decreasing FV expression), with the remaining being missense mutations (usually impairing FV secretion).

evidence.reference_title: Severe coagulation factor V deficiency caused by a 4 bp deletion in the factor V gene.
evidence.snippet: Sequence analysis of the 5'- and 3'-untranslated, coding and adjacent regions of the factor V gene revealed the presence of a 4 bp deletion in exon 13.

nodes.description: Easy bruising, a common spontaneous manifestation.

evidence.reference_title: Genetic and Clinical Characteristics of Russian Patients with Congenital Factor V Deficiency.
evidence.snippet: Clinically, congenital FV deficiency most commonly presents with epistaxis, easy bruising, hematomas, and menorrhagia.

nodes.description: Nosebleeds, among the most frequent presenting symptoms across cohorts.

evidence.reference_title: Symptoms of inherited factor V deficiency in 35 Iranian patients.
evidence.snippet: The most frequent symptoms included epistaxis and excessive bleeding after surgery.

nodes.description: A 2025 CRISPR knock-in carrying a missense variant chosen in silico to give a mild phenotype. Homozygotes are viable with no spontaneous bleeding, reduced factor V activity (around 24.5%) and prolonged PT and aPTT - the first viable pathological mouse model of the disease, usable for testing new therapies.

evidence.reference_title: Development of a novel and viable knock-in factor V deficiency murine model: Utility for an ultra-rare disease.
evidence.snippet: A viable FV-deficient mouse model was generated by introducing a missense mutation in FV. The model exhibits a mild phenotype of the disease, akin to that observed in humans.

nodes.description: The Cui et al. (1996) factor V knockout. About half of homozygous embryos die at embryonic day 9-10, possibly from a yolk-sac vascular abnormality; the rest reach term but die of massive haemorrhage within two hours of birth. The model established the absolute requirement for factor V in prothrombinase activity and revealed a developmental role for the coagulation system.

evidence.reference_title: Fatal haemorrhage and incomplete block to embryogenesis in mice lacking coagulation factor V.
evidence.snippet: The remaining Fv-/- mice progress normally to term, but die from massive haemorrhage within 2 hours of birth.

nodes.description: A factor V minigene expressed at under 0.1% of normal in the liver rescues Fv-/- mice through the perinatal period to adulthood without spontaneous haemorrhage, demonstrating that minimal factor V expression suffices for survival - a plausible explanation for why nearly all human patients retain some residual factor V.

evidence.reference_title: Rescue of fatal neonatal hemorrhage in factor V deficient mice by low level transgene expression.
evidence.snippet: Rescued Tg+,Fv-/- mice have undetectable FV (<0.1%) in both plasma and platelet compartments, but survive the perinatal period and mature to adulthood without spontaneous hemorrhage.

evidence.reference_title: Nationwide Study on Factor V Deficiency in China: Clinical Characteristics, Genotype, and Treatment Approaches.
evidence.snippet: The study cohort comprised 45 patients with confirmed FV:C reductions (undetectable to 48%), including six mild (FV:C >10%), 31 moderate (FV:C 1%-10%), and eight severe (FV:C <1%) patients.

readouts.description: FV:C measures the functional consequence of the genetic lesion at the level of circulating protein activity, and defines the conventional severity strata.

nodes.description: The mainstay of treatment, because no factor-V-specific concentrate is licensed. Plasma supplies intact factor V; dosing targets a haemostatic factor V level (commonly above 20 IU/dL), and because the plasma half-life of factor V is short, repeated infusions are needed. Virus-inactivated (solvent-detergent) plasma is preferred.

evidence.reference_title: Clinical, Laboratory, and Molecular Aspects of Factor V Deficiency.
evidence.snippet: The mainstay of treatment includes fresh-frozen plasma, preferentially virus-inactivated.

evidence.reference_title: Rare inherited coagulation disorders: no longer orphan and neglected.
evidence.snippet: Because of the relatively short plasma half-life of FV (16-36 hours), daily infusions are required to keep FV at hemostatic levels (ie, above 20 IU/dL)

nodes.description: Gastrointestinal bleeding, a rare but serious manifestation.

evidence.reference_title: Genetic and Clinical Characteristics of Russian Patients with Congenital Factor V Deficiency.
evidence.snippet: Severe manifestations, such as gastrointestinal bleeding, hematuria, hemarthrosis, or central nervous system hemorrhage, are relatively uncommon

nodes.description: Gum bleeding, the most common symptom in the Chinese national cohort (38.5%).

evidence.snippet: The most common symptoms included gingival (n = 15, 38.5%) and cutaneous bleeding (n = 13, 33.3%) in 39 patients.

nodes.description: Failure to form a stable fibrin network at sites of vascular injury. This is the step the routine coagulation screen measures, and it is why both the prothrombin time and the activated partial thromboplastin time are prolonged while the thrombin time, which tests the fibrinogen-to-fibrin step directly, remains normal.

evidence.reference_title: Factor V Deficiency.
evidence.snippet: Initial laboratory evaluation shows prolonged prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) with a normal thrombin time.

nodes.description: The non-redundant step. Activated factor V (factor Va) is the non-enzymatic cofactor of the prothrombinase complex, assembling with factor Xa on an anionic phospholipid surface and accelerating prothrombin cleavage far beyond what factor Xa achieves alone. Because both the extrinsic and intrinsic arms of the cascade converge on this common-pathway step, neither can compensate for the defect.

cell_types: activated platelet supplying the anionic phospholipid surface

evidence.reference_title: Factor V Deficiency.
evidence.snippet: Either thrombin or factor Xa converts factor V to the plasma cofactor of the prothrombinase complex. This complex, composed of calcium, phospholipids, factor Va, and factor Xa, is essential for converting prothrombin to thrombin.

nodes.description: The most feared complication, concentrated in neonates and infants with the lowest factor V levels and sometimes the presenting event.

evidence.snippet: Among the previous spontaneous intracranial hemorrhages in the congenital FV deficiency cases, most spontaneous intracranial hemorrhages occurred in infancy (13 of 20). All of the patients had FV activity less than 5% of normal.

nodes.description: Definitive cure for the most severe cases, since factor V is synthesised in the liver. Reserved for patients with life-threatening bleeding unmanageable by plasma; it corrects factor V levels and abolishes the need for infusions.

evidence.reference_title: Management of intracranial hemorrhage in severe factor V deficiency and definitive treatment with liver transplantation.
evidence.snippet: He received an orthotopic liver transplant at age 5 months, resulting in correction of his FV levels. He has not required any plasma infusions post-transplantation and has had no further bleeding episodes.

nodes.description: Factor-V-deficient plasma carries physiologically low levels of tissue factor pathway inhibitor, possibly because factor V affects TFPI stability or clearance in vivo. The reduced TFPI lowers the factor V threshold needed for minimal thrombin generation and so works alongside residual platelet factor V to protect deficient patients from severe bleeding.
nodes.id: Low Plasma Tissue Factor Pathway Inhibitor

evidence.reference_title: Low plasma levels of tissue factor pathway inhibitor in patients with congenital factor V deficiency.
evidence.snippet: Plasma TFPI antigen and activity levels were indeed lower (P < .001) in FV-deficient patients (n = 11; 4.0 +/- 1.0 ng/mL free TFPI) than in controls (n = 20; 11.5 +/- 4.8 ng/mL)

evidence.reference_title: Low plasma levels of tissue factor pathway inhibitor in patients with congenital factor V deficiency.
evidence.snippet: Low TFPI levels decreased the FV requirement for minimal thrombin generation in FV-deficient plasma to less than 1% and might therefore protect FV-deficient patients from severe bleeding.

molecular_functions: tissue factor pathway inhibitor serine protease inhibitor activity

nodes.description: Heavy menstrual bleeding, a common and sometimes dominant manifestation in affected women; present in 38.9% of reproductive-age women in the Chinese cohort.

evidence.reference_title: Nationwide Study on Factor V Deficiency in China: Clinical Characteristics, Genotype, and Treatment Approaches.
evidence.snippet: Menorrhagia (n = 7) was observed in 38.9% of 18 female patients of reproductive age.

nodes.description: Used when plasma alone is ineffective, exploiting the platelet factor V pool that localises to the site of bleeding. Platelet concentrates have been combined with plasma for refractory bleeding.

evidence.reference_title: Rare inherited coagulation disorders: no longer orphan and neglected.
evidence.snippet: a combination of platelet concentrates and SD-FFP has been used when SD-FFP alone was ineffective

nodes.description: Excessive bleeding at delivery in severely deficient women, controllable with plasma replacement.

evidence.snippet: patients with severe deficiency bleed considerably at the time of delivery. However, bleeding can be controlled properly by administration of fresh frozen plasma with excellent foetal outcome.

nodes.description: The convergence of residual platelet factor V and low TFPI: enough thrombin is generated at the activated platelet surface to secure a minimally haemostatic clot even when plasma factor V is undetectable. This is the mechanistic reason bleeding severity is discordant with plasma FV:C, and it is why a patient can be protected whose plasma assay reads zero.

nodes.description: The functional deficit measured in plasma as factor V coagulant activity (FV:C). In type I disease the immunoreactive antigen falls with it; in type II a dysfunctional molecule is still present at near-normal antigen. Residual activity grades the deficiency into mild, moderate and severe strata but predicts bleeding only weakly.

evidence.snippet: We have studied a young girl with very mild bleeding symptoms and undetectable levels of plasma factor V antigen and activity (<0.3% and <1.6% of normal, respectively).

evidence.reference_title: Functional characterization of a novel missense mutation, His147Arg, in A1 domain of FV protein causing type II deficiency.
evidence.snippet: The His147Arg mutation was associated with normal antigen levels, both in cell lysates and conditioned media, whereas FV activity was significantly reduced to 63.5 ± 17.0%.

molecular_functions: factor V cofactor available for prothrombinase assembly

nodes.description: The functional common denominator of the disease. Thrombin is needed both to cleave fibrinogen to fibrin and to amplify its own generation through feedback activation of factors V, VIII and XI, so a prothrombinase deficit propagates rather than being buffered.

evidence.reference_title: Low plasma levels of tissue factor pathway inhibitor in patients with congenital factor V deficiency.
evidence.snippet: Thrombin generation in FV-deficient plasma was only measurable at high tissue factor concentrations

nodes.description: About a fifth to a quarter of the body's factor V is stored in platelet alpha-granules, acquired by megakaryocyte endocytosis of plasma factor V rather than synthesised in the platelet. In patients with undetectable plasma factor V, a measurable platelet-derived factor V/Va pool can persist and be released locally at a wound, where it is the predominant cofactor for thrombin generation at the platelet surface. This pool, not any residual plasma factor V, is the leading explanation for the mild phenotype of many severely deficient patients.

cell_types: platelet storing factor V in alpha-granules

evidence.reference_title: Platelets and platelet-derived factor Va confer hemostatic competence in complete factor V deficiency.
evidence.snippet: release of the patient's platelet-derived FV/Va (7% of normal) following platelet activation resulted in robust thrombin generation, similar to that in an individual with normal plasma- and platelet-derived FV concentrations

evidence.reference_title: Residual platelet factor V ensures thrombin generation in patients with severe congenital factor V deficiency and mild bleeding symptoms.
evidence.snippet: patients with undetectable plasma FV may contain functional FV in their platelets. In combination with low TFPI level, residual platelet FV allows sufficient thrombin generation to rescue these patients from fatal bleeding.
